title: Ethics, Bias, and Responsible Data Science
summary: Data science has real power over people's lives, deciding who gets a loan, a job interview, or medical attention, so doing it responsibly is not optional. A central concern is bias: models learn from historical data, and if that data reflects past di
content:
# Ethics, Bias, and Responsible Data Science ##### The hiring model that learned to reject women Amazon built a resume-screening model trained on ten years of hiring decisions. It worked as designed: it learned the patterns in historical hiring. The problem was that historical hiring had favoured men. The model learned to penalise the word "women's" (as in "women's chess club captain") and to downgrade graduates of two all-women's colleges. Engineers removed those explicit signals. The model found proxies — verbs more common in men's resumes, activities correlated with gender. The project was abandoned in 2018. Nobody wrote a discriminatory rule. The model learned discrimination from data that encoded it, and it did so faithfully. That is the defining property of machine learning bias: **it does not require anyone's intent.** It requires only that history was unequal and that you trained on history. Data science now decides who gets a loan, an interview, a hospital bed, or a longer prison sentence. Doing it responsibly is not an optional module at the end of a course — and increasingly, under India's DPDP Act and sectoral RBI guidance, it is a legal requirement. ##### Where bias comes from Bias enters at several points, and knowing which one you have determines what will fix it. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Historical bias:
the world was unequal] --> D[Training data] B[Representation bias:
some groups undersampled] --> D C[Measurement bias:
the label is a flawed proxy] --> D D --> E[Model learns all of it faithfully] E --> F[Deployment bias:
used outside intended context] E --> G[Aggregation bias:
one model for distinct populations] F --> H[Decisions reshape future data] G --> H H --> D ``` **Historical bias** — the data accurately reflects a world that was unfair. Amazon's model was accurate about the past. **Representation bias** — some groups are undersampled. Facial recognition systems trained overwhelmingly on light-skinned faces showed error rates of 0.8% for lighter-skinned men and up to 34.7% for darker-skinned women in the Gender Shades study. The models were not designed to fail; they were tested on data where those failures were invisible. **Measurement bias** — the label is a proxy for what you actually care about, and the proxy is biased. This is the subtlest and most dangerous. A widely-used US healthcare algorithm used *healthcare spending* as a proxy for *health need*. Because less money was historically spent on Black patients with the same conditions, the algorithm systematically underestimated their need, affecting millions of people. **Aggregation bias** — one model applied to populations that behave differently. A credit model trained mostly on salaried urban borrowers applied to agricultural income in rural India will systematically misprice risk. **Feedback loops** — the model's decisions become tomorrow's training data. Predictive policing sends patrols to areas the model flagged; more patrols find more incidents; the model becomes more confident. The loop is self-confirming and self-reinforcing. **Removing the sensitive attribute does not remove bias.** Pincode correlates with community and caste. First names correlate with religion and region. Phone prefix correlates with income. A model without a `gender` column can still discriminate by gender through a dozen proxies. Test for this directly: ```python from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score # Can the remaining features predict the protected attribute? proxy_auc = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000), X.drop(columns=["gender"]), sensitive_attr, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean() print(f"Proxy leakage: gender predictable at AUC {proxy_auc:.3f}") # Anything well above 0.5 means proxies exist ``` ##### Measuring fairness Fairness is not one number, and the definitions conflict mathematically. ```python import pandas as pd, numpy as np from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix def fairness_report(y_true, y_pred, y_score, group): rows = [] for g in np.unique(group): m = group == g tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_true[m], y_pred[m], labels=[0, 1]).ravel() rows.append({ "group": g, "n": int(m.sum()), "base_rate": round(y_true[m].mean(), 4), # ground-truth rate "selection_rate": round(y_pred[m].mean(), 4), # demographic parity "tpr": round(tp / max(tp + fn, 1), 4), # equal opportunity "fpr": round(fp / max(fp + tn, 1), 4), # equalised odds "precision": round(tp / max(tp + fp, 1), 4), # predictive parity }) df = pd.DataFrame(rows) print(df.to_string(index=False)) print(f"\ndemographic parity difference: " f"{df.selection_rate.max() - df.selection_rate.min():.4f}") print(f"disparate impact ratio: " f"{df.selection_rate.min() / df.selection_rate.max():.4f}") print(f"equal opportunity difference: {df.tpr.max() - df.tpr.min():.4f}") return df fairness_report(y_test.values, y_pred, y_prob, X_test["gender"].values) ``` The main definitions: | Definition | Requires equal | Question it answers | |---|---|---| | **Demographic parity** | Selection rate | Are we approving the same proportion of each group? | | **Equal opportunity** | True positive rate | Among those who qualify, do we find them equally? | | **Equalised odds** | TPR *and* FPR | Are error rates equal in both directions? | | **Predictive parity** | Precision | When we say yes, are we right equally often? | | **Calibration** | P(actual \| score) | Does a score of 0.3 mean the same for everyone? | **These cannot all hold at once.** Chouldechova and Kleinberg et al. proved that when base rates differ between groups, calibration, equal false positive rates and equal false negative rates are mathematically incompatible. This was the substance of the COMPAS dispute. ProPublica's 2016 investigation showed Black defendants had roughly twice the false positive rate — labelled high-risk but not reoffending. Northpointe responded that the tool was equally calibrated across races, which was also true. Both analyses were correct. Because base rates differed, satisfying one definition guaranteed violating the other. **So you must choose, justify and document the choice.** A rough guide: use equal opportunity when missing a qualified person is the primary harm (hiring, medical screening); use equalised odds when false positives carry serious cost (criminal justice, fraud holds); use calibration when the score feeds a downstream expected-value calculation. The **four-fifths rule** — a disparate impact ratio below 0.8 — comes from US employment law and is widely used as a screening trigger. Treat it as a signal to investigate, not a legal standard; India's framework rests on constitutional non-discrimination principles plus sectoral regulation. Fairlearn packages this analysis: ```python from fairlearn.metrics import MetricFrame, selection_rate, true_positive_rate mf = MetricFrame( metrics={"selection_rate": selection_rate, "tpr": true_positive_rate}, y_true=y_test, y_pred=y_pred, sensitive_features=X_test[["gender", "region"]], # intersectional ) print(mf.by_group) print(mf.difference(method="between_groups")) ``` **Audit intersectionally.** Fairness holding for gender and for region separately does not mean it holds for women in Tier-3 towns. Gender Shades found exactly this — the intersectional gaps were far larger than the marginal ones. And always report subgroup sizes with confidence intervals. A 9-point gap on a subgroup of 140 people may be noise. ##### Mitigation Three intervention points, with different trade-offs. **Pre-processing** — reweight or resample the training data so groups are balanced. Model-agnostic. **In-processing** — add a fairness constraint during training. Usually the best accuracy-fairness trade-off: ```python from fairlearn.reductions import ExponentiatedGradient, EqualizedOdds mitigator = ExponentiatedGradient( estimator=LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000), constraints=EqualizedOdds(difference_bound=0.05), ) mitigator.fit(X_train, y_train, sensitive_features=A_train) ``` **Post-processing** — apply group-specific thresholds to a trained model. Simple and effective, and legally fraught: explicitly using a protected attribute at decision time may itself be unlawful in some jurisdictions and sectors. Get legal review before deploying it. Always report the cost. Produce the accuracy-fairness frontier rather than a single point, so stakeholders can see that reducing the TPR gap from 0.14 to 0.03 costs 1.8 points of AUC — and can decide whether that trade is acceptable. That decision belongs to legal, product and domain experts together, not to the data scientist alone. One thing no algorithm fixes: **if your label is biased, mitigation only redistributes the bias more evenly.** The healthcare-spending proxy needed a different label, not a fairness constraint. ##### Privacy and consent India's **Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023** governs personal data processing and creates obligations that directly constrain data science work: - **Lawful basis** — consent or a legitimate use for processing. - **Purpose limitation** — data collected for one purpose cannot be freely repurposed. Training a model on data collected for billing may not be covered. - **Data minimisation** — collect only what you need. - **Storage limitation** — delete when the purpose is served. - **Right to erasure** — individuals can require deletion. For a trained model this is genuinely hard, since the model arguably contains their data. - **Breach notification** — reportable to the Data Protection Board. Penalties reach ₹250 crore for failure to implement reasonable security safeguards. Practical measures: ```python import hashlib from presidio_analyzer import AnalyzerEngine, PatternRecognizer, Pattern from presidio_anonymizer import AnonymizerEngine analyzer, anonymizer = AnalyzerEngine(), AnonymizerEngine() # Presidio's defaults are US-centric — add Indian identifiers for entity, pattern, score in [ ("IN_AADHAAR", r"\b[2-9]\d{3}\s?\d{4}\s?\d{4}\b", 0.7), ("IN_PAN", r"\b[A-Z]{5}\d{4}[A-Z]\b", 0.85), ]: analyzer.registry.add_recognizer(PatternRecognizer( supported_entity=entity, patterns=[Pattern(entity.lower(), pattern, score)])) def pseudonymize_id(value: str, salt: str) -> str: return hashlib.sha256((salt + str(value)).encode()).hexdigest()[:16] df["customer_hash"] = df["phone"].map(lambda v: pseudonymize_id(v, SALT)) df = df.drop(columns=["phone", "email", "aadhaar", "full_name"]) ``` Two cautions. **Pseudonymisation is not anonymisation** — hashed IDs are still personal data under most frameworks, because they remain linkable. And **re-identification is easier than intuition suggests**: Sweeney's work showed that 87% of the US population was uniquely identifiable from ZIP code, birth date and sex alone. Removing names is not enough. Also relevant: never send raw PII to a third-party LLM API. Redact first, and log that you redacted. ##### Transparency and accountability If a model affects someone, they are owed an explanation. ```python import shap explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(model) sv = explainer(X_instance) shap.plots.waterfall(sv[0]) # why THIS decision ``` The distinction that matters: **global** interpretability validates the model (does it rely on legitimate factors? are there proxies?), while **local** interpretability justifies one decision (why was this application declined?). A rejected applicant needs the second, and a feature-importance bar chart does not provide it. **Counterfactuals** are the most actionable format: "had your average balance been ₹18,000 instead of ₹11,200, this would have been approved." Constrain them to features a person can actually change — a counterfactual suggesting someone be five years younger is worse than useless. Documentation is the accountability mechanism. Three artifacts: - **Model card** (Mitchell et al.) — intended use, out-of-scope uses, evaluation across subgroups, known limitations. - **Datasheet** (Gebru et al.) — how the data was collected, from whom, with what consent, what it omits. - **Impact assessment** — who could be harmed, how severely, and what controls exist. Mandatory under DPDP for Significant Data Fiduciaries. The sections that earn their keep are `out_of_scope`, `known_gaps`, and the *weakest* subgroup's performance. A card reporting only headline metrics is marketing. ##### Responsible practice as a habit Questions worth asking at each stage, before the work rather than after: **Framing** — who benefits, who bears the cost, and what happens to someone the model gets wrong? Is a model the right intervention at all? **Data** — was it collected with consent for this purpose? Who is missing from it? Does the label measure what I actually care about? **Modelling** — have I measured performance per subgroup? Can the remaining features predict the protected attribute? Which fairness definition am I choosing, and why? **Deployment** — is there a human in the loop for high-stakes decisions? Can an affected person get an explanation and appeal? Is fairness monitored after launch, not just before? That last point is routinely missed. Fairness measured once at launch says nothing about six months later, when the population has shifted. Audit on every retrain. And a genuinely important professional habit: **you are allowed to say no.** If a project is designed to do something you believe is harmful, raising it is part of the job. Document your concerns in writing. ##### Common mistakes - Believing that removing the sensitive attribute removes the bias. - Reporting only aggregate accuracy, hiding subgroup failures. - Auditing marginally and missing much larger intersectional gaps. - Picking a fairness metric without knowing the others exist or conflict. - Applying a fairness constraint when the *label* was the biased artifact. - Reporting a subgroup gap with no confidence interval on a small group. - Treating pseudonymised data as anonymous. - Using Presidio's default recognizers, missing Aadhaar and PAN. - Auditing fairness at launch and never again. - Deploying group-specific thresholds without legal review. ##### Hands-on Take a model you built earlier and split its performance by a sensitive attribute — gender, region, age band, or an available proxy. Compute selection rate, TPR, FPR and precision per group, along with base rates and subgroup sizes. Add bootstrap confidence intervals so you can distinguish a real gap from noise. Then run the proxy-leakage test: train a classifier to predict the protected attribute from your remaining features, and see how well it does. Write up what you find, including the base rates, because differing base rates are why your fairness metrics will conflict. For the mini-project, conduct a full fairness audit on a dataset with a sensitive attribute. Measure at least four fairness definitions, do an intersectional breakdown across two attributes, apply one mitigation technique, and plot the accuracy-fairness frontier rather than reporting a single mitigated point. Write a short assessment naming which definition you would prioritise for this use case and why, what the mitigation cost, and what you could *not* fix with modelling — because the honest answer usually includes something about the data or the label. For the assignment, find a real case where a data or AI system caused harm through bias or a privacy failure. COMPAS, Amazon's hiring tool, the Optum healthcare algorithm, Gender Shades, and several Aadhaar-linked data exposures are all well documented. Analyse what went wrong mechanically — which type of bias, at which stage — and what specific practice would have caught it before deployment. ##### Key takeaways - Bias enters through historical, representation, measurement and aggregation pathways; models learn all of it faithfully. - Removing the protected attribute does not remove discrimination — proxies are pervasive, so test for them directly. - Fairness definitions conflict mathematically when base rates differ; you must choose, justify and document. - Audit intersectionally with subgroup sizes and confidence intervals, and re-audit on every retrain. - Under DPDP, pseudonymised data is still personal data — and documentation plus a human appeal route is what accountability actually means.
